proposals.relationship: Darnton acknowledges borrowing Douglas’s ideas when developing his anthropological approach to historical meaning.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2024 theory answer expressly identifies Mary Douglas among borrowed intellectual resources. Own 2021 anthropology answer gives her pangolin as a concrete example of meaningful things woven into ritual and cultural patterns, alongside Turner and Evans-Pritchard. This is a plural, critically interpreted debt, not formal instruction or identification of an unread original Douglas title. Darnton rejects a mechanical anthropological toolkit.

proposals.relationship: Darnton uses Goffman’s definition of situations to interpret theatrical metaphors and collective perceptions in prerevolutionary Paris.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2021 answer names The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life and distinguishes an initial superficial role-playing reading from a later, more useful account of defining a situation. He connects it specifically to accounts of 1787–1788 and a work then in progress. Own 2024 answer confirms theatrical communication as a resource for The Revolutionary Temper. This is his attributed use, not independent verification of Goffman’s book or every historical episode.

proposals.relationship: Darnton credits Durkheim’s collective-consciousness concept when explaining The Revolutionary Temper’s account of shared historical perceptions.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2024 theory answer explicitly attributes collective consciousness to Durkheim and says he made this theoretical acknowledgment more visible because the book’s title required explanation. This is a specific conceptual resource rather than a claim that all readers think alike, a verified single cause of revolution, or adherence to an entire sociological school. No particular original Durkheim work is identified or newly read; the existing group Social facts and collective life node is distinct from the person endpoint.

proposals.relationship: Darnton credits Furet’s group with drawing him into serial book history while extending its source base to illegal literature.

proposals.relationship: Darnton credits Chartier’s work on readers’ active appropriation while retaining doubts about the evidentiary reach of reading history.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2021 reading-history answer explicitly says he follows Chartier in taking inspiration from de Certeau and the other named reader theorist. He is persuaded by Chartier’s insights while distinguishing suggestive findings from a fully documented history. This resource coexists with his particular criticism and the 2024 insistence on substantial shared ground. The source’s spelling of the second intermediary is not treated as a new identity; no Chartier book or original discussion is freshly read.

proposals.relationship: Darnton questions the evidence available for a systematic history of reading and disputes the claim that the Revolution invented the Enlightenment.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2021 answer praises Chartier’s insights but says sparse sources leave aperçus rather than a demonstrated history of reading. Own 2024 answer recounts their disagreement over The Cultural Origins of the French Revolution, maintaining that an Enlightenment force existed before 1789 while agreeing that later revolutionary legitimation mattered. He explicitly rejects simple book-to-action causation for both scholars and is unsure they have a fundamental difference. These are particular, dated objections in a friendly exchange, not rejection of all Chartier research or a fresh reading of his book.

proposals.relationship: Darnton explicitly takes inspiration from de Certeau’s active reader, through his engagement with Chartier’s work.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2021 reading-history answer identifies Chartier’s mediation and de Certeau’s account of readers finding meanings unintended by authors. proposals.relationship: Darnton asks how the reader-as-poacher model can yield demonstrable collective tendencies rather than endlessly varied individual readings.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2021 reading-history answer raises the problem conditionally after explicitly crediting de Certeau. He considers Fish’s interpretive communities as a possible response, then asks how they can be located with evidence. This is a particular limit on the historical application of the model, not a claim that de Certeau denied social pattern or that Chartier endorses absolute reader freedom. The existing group route preserves Chartier’s own rejection of that absolute-freedom interpretation; original books remain unread.

proposals.relationship: Darnton invokes Lévi-Strauss’s account of thinking with concrete things when explaining his interpretive approach to historical cultures.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2021 anthropology answer explicitly credits the demonstration that people combine concrete things in thought, then gives distinct Douglas, Turner and Evans-Pritchard examples. This is his specific conceptual resource, not adherence to all structuralism or evidence that each anthropologist offered an interchangeable method. proposals.relationship: Darnton challenges the applicability of Habermas’s rational public sphere to eighteenth-century Parisian songs, rumors and noisy exchanges.
proposals.evidence_note: In his own published 2024 answer Darnton expresses admiration for Habermas while contrasting a sober rational-discussion model with shouting, singing, stories, market disputes, scandals and gossip in eighteenth-century France. The objection concerns historical application and forms of public communication, not a denial that public opinion existed. He identifies a sympathetic parallel criticism by Farge. Habermas’s original text and Farge’s original response are not newly read, and no exact original title is inferred.

proposals.relationship: Darnton explicitly aligns his account of noisy Parisian public opinion with Farge’s sympathetic criticism of Habermas.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2024 answer says his perspective coincides with Farge’s criticism that Habermas misrepresents the public presentation of ideas: cafés and markets, songs, gossip, scandals and rumors rather than only sober rational discussion. This is a specific attributed methodological comparison, not proof that Farge caused Darnton’s approach or an independent reading of her original argument. Darnton preserves admiration for Habermas and the existence of public opinion.
